strengths: Proposes a novel 'iterative paradigm' for story visualization that is conceptually distinct from existing Auto-Regressive and Reference-Image paradigms, using all previously generated images as evolving global references rather than fixed or local ones, which plausibly reduces error accumulation and propagation of reference-image flaws.

The proposed Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA) module is training-free and plug-and-play, reusing pretrained cross-attention weights, and is shown to scale much better in FLOPs than Consistent Self-Attention (CSA) as the number of reference images grows.

Extensive empirical evaluation across regular-length (StorySalon) and long-story (up to 100 frames) settings, with quantitative metrics (CLIP-T, aCCS, aFID), qualitative comparisons, ablations on initialization/GRCA/iteration schedule, and human evaluation, plus an additional comparison against subject-consistent generation baselines (IP-Adapter, PhotoMaker, StoryDiffusion).
Reasonably comprehensive appendix with additional analyses (effect of number of iterations, different visual styles, more qualitative examples) that supports the paper's central claims.
Clear visual evidence (e.g., Fig. 1, 4, 5, 7) that the method better preserves fine-grained interactions and subject identity compared to StoryDiffusion and StoryGen in several showcased examples.
weaknesses: The iterative paradigm requires L=10 full diffusion passes (each with 50 DDIM steps) over the entire story to refine all frames, which represents a substantial multiplicative increase in wall-clock generation cost compared to single-pass baselines (StoryDiffusion, StoryGen); the paper's efficiency claims and FLOPs comparisons (Fig. 8) only address per-image attention cost with varying numbers of references, not the total end-to-end computational/time budget across iterations, leaving the actual efficiency trade-off unclear or potentially unfavorable.

Table 6 reports aFID with an upward arrow (↑) while aFID is defined as Fréchet Inception Distance elsewhere in the paper with a downward-better convention (↓); this inconsistency is confusing and raises questions about whether the metric or its interpretation is correctly reported, undermining confidence in the reported ablation trends.

For the long-story setting, stories and descriptions are synthesized via GPT-4o without real ground-truth images, making it unclear how aFID/aCCS are computed (i.e., what serves as the reference distribution), which raises reproducibility and validity concerns for this core evaluation.

The linear weighting schedule for λ (0.3 to 0.5) and the choice of 10 iterations appear to be tuned heuristically based on the same benchmarks used for evaluation, with limited principled justification or sensitivity analysis beyond a coarse ablation.

Comparisons are largely restricted to a small set of relatively recent but not exhaustive baselines (StoryGen, StoryDiffusion, AR-LDM, IP-Adapter, PhotoMaker); several other recent story-visualization methods discussed in the related work (e.g., StoryImager, AutoStory, TheaterGen) are not included in the quantitative comparison, weakening claims of state-of-the-art superiority.

Human evaluation protocol details (number of participants, inter-rater agreement, statistical significance) are not reported, limiting the ability to assess the robustness of the reported preference scores.
Minor presentation issues, such as a placeholder 'https URL' in the abstract instead of an actual project link, reduce polish and could hint at incomplete preparation for submission.

strengths: The proposed iterative paradigm (using all previously generated frames as global reference rather than only past frames or fixed initial frames) is a reasonable conceptual contribution that addresses real failure modes (error accumulation in AR methods, propagation of reference-image flaws in RI methods).
Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA) is training-free and plug-and-play, reusing pretrained IP-Adapter cross-attention weights, which is appealing from a practicality standpoint.

The paper provides an extensive set of experiments: regular-length (StorySalon) and self-curated long-story (up to 100 frames) settings, ablations on initialization, GRCA vs. CSA, iteration count, and weighting schedule, plus a human study and a subject-consistent generation comparison.
Qualitative figures illustrate plausible improvements in fine-grained multi-character interactions (e.g., 'greeting', 'lifting') compared to StoryDiffusion/StoryGen in several cherry-picked examples.
weaknesses: The claim of 'consistently outperforms existing methods' is not well supported by the paper's own tables. In Table 1 (regular-length), the base Story-Adapter has a worse aFID (16.80) than StoryDiffusion (14.84), and even Story-AdapterXL only marginally beats StoryDiffusion on aFID (14.63 vs 14.84), essentially a tie, while CLIP-T is also roughly tied (0.310 vs 0.311). In Table 2 (long story), IP-AdapterXL achieves a substantially better (lower) aFID than Story-AdapterXL (58.69 vs 94.30), directly contradicting the narrative that the proposed iterative method 'significantly improves semantic consistency' -- the paper only offers a post-hoc, somewhat unconvincing explanation (fixed reference images give lower FID) rather than acknowledging this as a real trade-off/limitation.

The efficiency claims ('training-free and computationally efficient framework') are misleading. The iterative paradigm requires re-running the full diffusion sampling process (e.g., 50 DDIM steps) once per iteration for every image in the story, with 10 iterations by default (Algorithm 1), i.e., roughly a 10x increase in total denoising compute compared to single-pass AR or RI baselines such as StoryGen or StoryDiffusion. The paper's computational-cost comparison (Fig. 8) only benchmarks the attention module (GRCA vs. CSA) in isolation and does not report the overall wall-clock time or total FLOPs of the full iterative pipeline versus baselines, which substantially understates the real cost of the method.

The 'long story' evaluation set (20 stories generated via GPT-4o, 10 with 50-sentence descriptions and 10 with 100-sentence descriptions) is a small, self-curated benchmark with no public release details, no diversity analysis, and potential circularity since GPT-4o is used both to create prompts and (in related work) as an evaluator elsewhere in the community; this makes the long-story quantitative results difficult to reproduce or independently verify.

The core technical idea -- pooling all previous frames into global CLIP-image-embedding tokens and cross-attending to them, combined with a linearly increasing weighting factor λ over iterations -- is an incremental combination of existing components (IP-Adapter style cross-attention + iterative refinement + reference propagation), and the novelty relative to prior consistency modules (CSA, IP-Adapter) is limited.

Ablations show an inherent semantic-consistency vs. text-alignment trade-off that is not resolved: increasing λ or iteration count improves aCCS/aFID but degrades CLIP-T (Table 3, Table 6), and the paper picks a fixed operating point (10 iterations, λ from 0.3 to 0.5) without a principled justification beyond an empirical sweep on a small set of cases.

Human evaluation (Table 5) lacks basic methodological details such as number of annotators, inter-rater agreement, or statistical significance testing, making it hard to assess the reliability of the reported preference gaps, some of which (e.g., Story-Adapter vs. StoryDiffusion on several axes) are quite small.

The abstract's headline numbers ('9.4% improvement in aCCS and 21.71 reduction in aFID') do not clearly correspond to the numbers reported in Tables 1/2, and it is unclear which baseline/configuration these percentages are computed against, reducing clarity and reproducibility of the central quantitative claims.

Several qualitative comparison figures (e.g., Fig. 1, Fig. 4, Fig. 5) appear to be selected favorable examples without corresponding failure-case analysis for Story-Adapter itself, making it hard to gauge robustness across the full test distribution.

strengths: Introduces a novel iterative paradigm for long story visualization that uses all previously generated images as global references, addressing weaknesses of both auto-regressive (error accumulation) and reference-image (fixed reference propagation, no emerging character support) paradigms.

The proposed Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA) module is training-free/plug-and-play, reuses pretrained cross-attention weights, and operates on compact global CLIP embeddings rather than dense intermediate features, giving much better computational scaling with sequence length than CSA (as shown in the FLOPs comparison in Fig. 8).

Extensive empirical validation: quantitative comparisons on regular-length (StorySalon) and long (up to 100-frame, GPT-4o generated) story benchmarks against multiple strong baselines (StoryGen, StoryDiffusion, AR-LDM, IP-Adapter/IP-AdapterXL), plus a separate subject-consistent generation comparison against IP-Adapter/PhotoMaker/StoryDiffusion.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the effects of initialization, GRCA vs. CSA, the iterative paradigm, the linear weighting strategy, and the number of iterations, with both quantitative tables and qualitative figures.
Human evaluation study across three settings (subject-consistent generation, regular-length, and long story visualization) corroborates the automatic metrics.
Method is applicable to different base models (SD, SDXL via IP-Adapter weights) and different visual styles (cartoon and realistic), demonstrating some generality.
weaknesses: The long-story benchmark (GPT-4o generated 20 stories) is a benchmark curated by the authors themselves rather than an established public benchmark, which raises concerns about potential bias in prompt selection and limits reproducibility/comparability with future work.

Improvements in aFID/aCCS for long stories, while consistent, are sometimes modest relative to strong baselines (e.g., IP-AdapterXL is very close to Story-AdapterXL on CLIP-T and aCCS in Table 2), and no statistical significance or variance information is reported across the 20 curated stories.

The linear weighting strategy (λ increasing from 0.3 to 0.5) and number of iterations (10) appear to be hand-tuned hyperparameters without a principled or automatic selection procedure; Table 6 shows text-image alignment (CLIP-T) monotonically degrades with more iterations, suggesting a consistency/controllability trade-off that is not deeply analyzed or theoretically justified.

Computational cost is discussed only in terms of FLOPs relative to CSA; wall-clock inference time/latency for the full iterative pipeline (which requires ~10 full re-generations of the entire story) is not reported, which is important given the method needs multiple full diffusion passes over the whole story instead of a single pass.

The paper claims scalability to long stories (up to 100 frames) but all reference images must be stored and reprocessed via CLIP encoding at every iteration for every frame; memory/storage scaling with very long stories (e.g., beyond 100 frames) is not analyzed.

Some qualitative comparisons (e.g., Fig. 4, Fig. 10) are cherry-picked single examples per baseline failure mode, which, combined with reliance on CLIP-based automatic metrics (CLIP-T, aFID, aCCS also built on CLIP/DINO-like features per Cheng et al. 2024), may not fully capture fine-grained interaction quality that the paper claims to improve.

The technical contribution is somewhat incremental: GRCA is largely an application of cross-attention with CLIP global embeddings (similar in spirit to IP-Adapter) combined with an iterative refinement loop; the core novelty is more in the overall iterative paradigm/system design than in a fundamentally new architectural or theoretical mechanism.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually clear third paradigm (external iterative refinement using full-length sequence as reference) that is well motivated relative to AR and fixed-reference paradigms, and is training-free/plug-and-play (reuses IP-Adapter cross-attention weights), making it easy to deploy.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: regular-length StorySalon benchmark, a newly curated long-story benchmark (up to 100 frames), human evaluation, subject-consistent generation comparisons, and comparisons against a wide range of baselines (AR-LDM, StoryGen, StoryDiffusion, ConsiStory, IP-Adapter/XL, PhotoMaker, and even reference-image-based editing models like FLUX.1 Kontext and Nano-Banana).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of GRCA, the iterative paradigm, the initialization step, the linear weighting schedule, and comparisons of GRCA vs. CSA and simpler aggregation baselines (sliding window, random reference, mean-pooled embedding), which support the design choices.
Practical variants (Story-Iter-Fast with SDXL-LCM, Story-Iter-ControlNet with pose conditioning) demonstrate extensibility and partially address the method's computational overhead.
Reasonable attempt at reproducibility: pseudocode (Algo. 1), detailed implementation section, and a stated commitment to release code.
weaknesses: The iterative paradigm incurs substantial computational overhead (e.g., 250 minutes vs. 31 minutes for StoryDiffusion on a 100-frame story), and while a fast variant is proposed, it comes with a CLIP-T/aFID trade-off, so the core method's practicality for very long stories remains a concern.

Quantitative gains over strong baselines are often marginal or mixed rather than clearly dominant: e.g., in Table 2 Story-IterXL's aFID (94.30) is worse than IP-AdapterXL (88.69) and SEED-LLaMA (88.96), and its CLIP-T (0.318) is close to ConsiStory/StoryDiffusion (0.315-0.316), undercutting the claim of clear state-of-the-art performance.

The paper itself documents a consistency/text-alignment trade-off that worsens with more iterations (Table 11, Sec. F), and qualitative examples in the appendix (e.g., Fig. 19) still show wrong/missing interactions even at high iteration counts, suggesting the method does not fully resolve fine-grained interaction issues it targets.

The long-story benchmark is self-constructed via GPT-4o with only 20 stories, which limits diversity/statistical robustness and reproducibility relative to an established, community-vetted benchmark; the aCCS/aFID metrics also depend on Grounding-DINO detections whose reliability for this purpose is not independently validated beyond citation to the authors' own prior work.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core technical contribution (GRCA) is largely a repurposing of IP-Adapter's decoupled cross-attention combined with global CLIP embeddings and an outer refinement loop, rather than a fundamentally new architecture, and conceptually resembles iterative/self-refinement ideas already present in the diffusion literature.

Limited discussion of failure modes and variance/robustness across random seeds or diverse story genres; the extensive appendix, while thorough, dilutes focus and some results (e.g., efficiency scaling to 200 frames) are only briefly mentioned without full experimental support.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and under-explored problem: maintaining semantic consistency in very long (up to 100-frame) story visualization, going beyond typical short story-visualization benchmarks.

Extremely thorough set of experiments and ablations (weighting strategy, GRCA vs CSA, number of iterations, GRCA component ablations, human evaluation, efficiency analysis, subject-consistent generation comparison, comparisons with reference-editing models like FLUX.1 Kontext/Nano-Banana), which shows the authors probed many angles of their design.

The proposed external iterative refinement (re-generating the whole story sequence conditioned on the previous round's full-length outputs) is a reasonably intuitive idea and is demonstrated to be plug-and-play/training-free by reusing pretrained IP-Adapter cross-attention weights.
Multiple practical variants are explored (Story-Iter-Fast with LCM backbone, Story-Iter-ControlNet with pose conditioning), suggesting some generality of the approach.
Qualitative results generally look visually appealing and the paper provides an extensive gallery of long-story examples in different styles.
weaknesses: Severe efficiency cost that undermines the core claims: generating a single 100-frame story with Story-Iter takes ~250 minutes (10 full external iterations, each running a full 50-step diffusion pass over all frames), versus 31 minutes for StoryDiffusion and far less for single-pass editing baselines (Table 3, Table 9). The paper's FLOPs/VRAM-based efficiency argument is misleading relative to actual wall-clock cost, which is the practically relevant metric; the "Fast" variant only partially mitigates this and trades off quality (aFID rises from 94.30 to 109.13).

Modest technical novelty: GRCA is essentially IP-Adapter's decoupled cross-attention (whose weights are directly reused without any modification/training) applied globally across all frames instead of one reference image, combined with an external iterative loop and a hand-tuned linear weighting schedule. The core architectural contribution is incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Consistency-alignment trade-off is a real and acknowledged limitation (Table 11, Sec. F): as iterations increase, aCCS/aFID improve but CLIP-T (text alignment) drops noticeably, and even at the "optimal" setting, Story-Iter's CLIP-T is often lower than the plain SDM baseline (Table 1: 0.303 vs. 0.323) and close to or below several competitors — the method appears to sacrifice text fidelity for visual consistency without a principled mechanism to balance the two, relying instead on a hand-tuned, iteration-count-specific linear schedule (λ_L, λ_ℓ) that likely needs re-tuning per story length/iteration count.

The long-story benchmark is self-curated using GPT-4o with no external validation, human-annotation protocol, or public release confirmation beyond a promise, raising reproducibility and evaluation-validity concerns for the paper's central long-story claims.
Human evaluation protocol is under-specified (number of participants, inter-rater agreement, statistical significance not reported), limiting the strength of the human-preference claims in Table 8.

Comparisons against strong recent reference-editing models (FLUX.1 Kontext, Nano-Banana) are somewhat apples-to-oranges since those are not designed for story visualization, and the paper's framing of their failures (rigid identity preservation) partly sidesteps that these models were not built for this open-ended multi-character task; this weakens the significance of claiming superiority over them.

Some result inconsistencies/framing issues: e.g., "w/o Initialization" achieves the best aFID in the ablation table (Table 4, 90.30 vs Story-Iter's 94.30), which is glossed over rather than fully reconciled with the paper's narrative about initialization's benefits.

The approach's dependence on repeatedly regenerating the entire story from scratch each iteration (rather than a more surgical/local refinement) seems computationally wasteful for long stories and raises scalability questions beyond the tested 100–200 frame range.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear conceptual gap between existing Auto-Regressive and Reference-Image paradigms for story visualization and proposes a well-motivated third paradigm (external iterative refinement using all previously generated frames as references), which is intuitive and clearly explained with illustrative diagrams (Fig. 2, 11).

The proposed Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA) module is training-free and plug-and-play, reusing pretrained IP-Adapter weights, making the method practical and easy to adopt without additional training cost.

Extensive empirical evaluation across regular-length (StorySalon) and long-story (up to 100 frames) settings, with comparisons to a wide range of relevant baselines (AR-LDM, StoryGen, StoryDiffusion, IP-Adapter, ConsiStory, and even modern reference-based editing models like FLUX.1 Kontext and Nano-Banana).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of initialization, GRCA vs. CSA, iteration count, weighting strategy, and alternative reference aggregation schemes (sliding window, random reference set, mean pooling), which support the design choices convincingly.
Human evaluation is included in addition to automatic metrics (CLIP-T, aCCS, aFID), strengthening the empirical claims.
Practical extensions (Story-Iter-Fast using LCM backbone, Story-Iter-ControlNet for pose control) demonstrate the flexibility and applicability of the proposed framework beyond the base setting.
The paper introduces a new long-story benchmark (up to 100 frames), addressing a gap in existing evaluation protocols which mostly focus on shorter stories.

Good transparency regarding limitations (diversity trade-off, alignment-consistency trade-off with more iterations, computational cost) and reasonably thorough appendix with pseudocode, additional qualitative comparisons, and efficiency analysis.
weaknesses: The iterative paradigm requires multiple full denoising passes across the whole story (e.g., 10 external iterations x 50 diffusion steps), leading to substantial computational cost (~250 minutes for a 100-frame, 1024-resolution story), which is higher than several baselines; the "efficiency" framing in places is somewhat optimistic relative to the reported wall-clock times.

The self-curated long-story benchmark (generated via GPT-4o and evaluated by the authors' own aCCS/aFID pipeline built on Grounding-DINO detections) lacks independent validation or human-annotated ground truth, raising some concern about potential evaluation bias, though the authors do plan to release the benchmark.

There is an acknowledged unresolved trade-off between semantic consistency and text-image alignment as iterations increase (Table 11), and between consistency and intra-story diversity (Sec. G); the paper flags but does not fully solve these issues.

The core cross-attention mechanism largely repurposes IP-Adapter's decoupled cross-attention weights, which somewhat limits the technical novelty of GRCA itself; the primary contribution is more at the level of the iterative paradigm/system design than a fundamentally new attention mechanism.

The linear weighting schedule for λ_i is tuned via ablation on a specific dataset/setting (Table 5); it is unclear how sensitive/generalizable this hyperparameter choice is across different story lengths, content types, or diffusion backbones.

Some quantitative comparisons (e.g., against single-image subject-consistent baselines or reference-editing models not designed for multi-frame narrative generation) may not be entirely apples-to-apples, even though the authors provide reasonable qualitative justification for these comparisons.
